Incorporating SLOOS signals, the tone remains cautiously constructive but with a slightly more restrained tilt than the baseline FOMC read.

What SLOOS adds:
- Business credit supply: Domestic banks report C&I lending standards largely unchanged now, with expectations to ease ahead (competition cited), and anticipate improved C&I asset quality. This supports the constructive macro view.
- Household credit: Banks expect to ease standards for residential mortgages (GSE-eligible and jumbo), with improving asset quality in nonconforming jumbo and subprime segments and little change for GSE and HELOCs—supportive for household spending.
- Areas of tightening/risk: Banks expect tighter standards for CRE (including construction/land development) and auto loans, and they expect asset-quality deterioration in credit cards and autos, signaling consumer-credit headwinds and property-sector vulnerability.
- Foreign banks: Expect tighter standards for C&I (especially for small firms) and CRE, with weaker business-loan demand and deteriorating multifamily asset quality—an additional drag on credit availability at the margin.

Net: SLOOS suggests a mixed credit backdrop—domestic easing in C&I and mortgages offsets but does not fully counter tighter CRE/auto and foreign-bank tightening. Combined with still-low market-based inflation compensation, this warrants a slightly more cautious tilt than the initial assessment.
